source.title: U-shaped and Inverted-U Scaling behind Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures and forecasts downstream task performance across model scale, rather than testing the original pretraining-loss scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior training-loss scaling laws but does not itself measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit parameter/token/compute power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter-token allocations. Its own relevant results concern downstream task metrics and forecasts. Results attributed to cited work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures downstream task performance of 56 existing LLMs against log training compute and forecasts accuracy past an emergence threshold from smaller models only. That bears directly on V6. It neither measures nor fits pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors show U-shaped scaling for hard questions and inverted-U followed by improvement for easy questions on six emergent multiple-choice tasks, offer this as a possible explanation of emergence, and propose Slice-and-Sandwich to predict the threshold and post-threshold performance. They caution that not all emergent tasks may show the pattern and that string-match tasks need a suitable continuous metric.
record.recipe_differences: The study groups downstream questions by difficulty, evaluates continuous and traditional task metrics across existing models, and fits polynomial forecasts. It does not reproduce the original pretraining-loss scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Forecast quality depends on polynomial degree, train-test compute threshold, and question-group count. The paper reports that higher polynomial degrees can overfit, and that degree 3 fits Persian-QA's easy group too flatly; it also reports an exception for the MMLU degree-5 fit at threshold 1.3.
record.problems: Most results are presented as plots and qualitative descriptions without numeric forecast errors or uncertainty estimates. The paper itself notes that clear difficulty-stratified patterns may not occur on all emergent benchmarks and that its string-match analysis is preliminary. The main text and appendix conflict over the easy-versus-hard pattern directions for Hindu knowledge and conceptual combinations.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant numeric results were omitted. Figure-only values were not estimated from plots.

untested.parts: Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss; models trained in a controlled scaling series (it uses heterogeneous off-the-shelf models).
All (it extrapolates downstream accuracy, not pretraining loss)
All (fit-sensitivity is shown only for its downstream polynomial forecasts)

missing.what: Analogical similarity forecast: Slice-and-Sandwich predicts emergence (slightly overestimated); the Sigmoid baseline gives a flat line
Robustness of forecasts: degree 7 (easy) and degrees 4/6 (hard) forecast poorly; degree 3 is too flat for Persian-QA; MMLU fails at threshold 1.3 with degree 5; results are robust to G
Hard-Lift alternative: better than baseline on MMLU and Persian-QA, worse on arithmetic
Accuracy correlates with TC Brier Score (Pearson 0.99/1.00/0.88) more strongly than with the unconditioned score (0.96/0.93/0.60)
Difficulty grouping on accuracy: inverted-U persists for easy groups, but hard groups stagnate near zero

record.verdict_notes: Forecast evidence is qualitative and plot-based, with no error metrics or uncertainty. The emergence threshold is set manually from accuracy, and the fitting degrees are chosen by prior belief about the curve shape. Compute estimates come from Ruan et al.; the models are heterogeneous families, not a controlled scaling series.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
It does not test whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs' held-out pretraining loss.
It does not test loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
It does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
It does not test scaling laws in other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests downstream benchmark performance across scale and forecasts it from smaller-scale models, but does not test predictability from pretraining loss.
The study discusses sensitivity of its own downstream polynomial forecasting procedure, not fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations for pretraining-loss scaling laws.

rows.value: The authors report inverted-U scaling followed by steady improvement for easy questions, and U-shaped scaling for hard questions.
rows.note: One aggregate result over the evaluated models; no per-model numeric values are given in the text.
rows.check: 'Observed' describes the paper's U/inverted-U pattern, not V6. Relative to V6, aggregate MMLU accuracy stagnates and then jumps (Fig 1a), and group-level scaling is non-monotonic, so predictable improvement holds only partly.

relationships.condition: Slice-and-Sandwich accuracy forecasts on MMLU and arithmetic, using only models below the threshold
relationships.reason: The authors state the forecasts capture the post-threshold soar, though only qualitatively (r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: Forecasts using only models below the threshold qualitatively capture the subsequent sharp accuracy gains on MMLU and arithmetic.

relationships.reason: Performance improves consistently with compute in most difficulty groups (r10).
relationships.display_finding: Performance improves consistently with compute in most difficulty groups for abstract narrative understanding.

relationships.condition: Emergent multiple-choice and string-match tasks, raw aggregate accuracy
relationships.reason: Accuracy stagnates and then jumps, and difficulty groups scale non-monotonically; a naive Sigmoid fit misses the soar (r1-r3, r6, r13).
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate accuracy stagnated before jumping, difficulty groups scaled non-monotonically, and a naive sigmoid fit failed to capture the surge.

relationships.condition: Easiest and hardest groups on ARC and HellaSwag
relationships.reason: These groups show flat scaling rather than improvement (r11, r12).
relationships.display_finding: The easiest and hardest ARC and HellaSwag groups showed flat performance as scale increased.

relationships.condition: Continuous metrics (TED, MCS) on word unscramble
relationships.reason: TED flattens and MCS is inverted-U; neither maps usefully to exact match (r14, r15).
relationships.display_finding: TED flattened and MCS followed an inverted U, with neither providing a useful mapping to exact match.

relationships.condition: Forecast fitting choices (polynomial degree, train-test threshold)
relationships.reason: Based on the text (App G): higher degrees and some thresholds forecast poorly, and Hard-Lift beats the baseline on MMLU and Persian-QA but not arithmetic. No row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Higher polynomial degrees and some fitting thresholds forecast poorly, while Hard-Lift beat the baseline on MMLU and Persian-QA but not arithmetic.
